title: How Ben Franklin planned to turn 1,000 pounds into 4 million
description:
In a 1789 codicil to his will, Benjamin Franklin left 1,000 pounds each to Boston and Philadelphia, to be lent to young tradesmen at 5% a year. At 5% money doubles about every 14 years, so after 100 years it is about 131 times bigger: 131,000 pounds. Franklin planned to spend 100,000 and lend the other 31,000 for another century: 31,000 x 131 = 4,061,000 pounds, his exact figure. The real funds fell short of the plan, but Boston's still reached almost $5 million by 1990.

Numbers checked in code (5% compounding year by year). Sources: Franklin's codicil (cs.appstate.edu/sjg/class/1010/wc/finance/benfcodicil.html), Wikipedia: Benjamin Franklin, Bequest.

beats.say: Your 1,000 pounds becomes 4 million, after you're gone.
No stocks, no luck. Just 5% and patience. Ben Franklin put it in his will in 1789.
Step one: lend it to young tradesmen at 5%. They repay a tenth a year, and you lend it again.
Step two: never spend the interest. Year one earns 50. The next year, 52 and a half. Interest on interest.
But that only doubles every 14 years. Can it reach millions?
Step three: wait. 100 years is 7 doublings, about 131 times. 131,000 pounds.
Step four: spend 100,000 on your town. Lend the last 31,000 for another century.
131 times again: 4,061,000 pounds. Franklin's own number. The real funds fell short, but Boston's still reached almost 5 million dollars.
Your turn: 1,000 pounds at 5%, untouched for 300 years. How much?
